claim: Neutrophils infiltrate the mouse liver following a circadian pattern in steady state.
source: Here, we demonstrated that in steady state, neutrophils infiltrated the mouse liver following a circadian pattern and regulated hepatocyte clock-genes by neutrophil elastase (NE) secretion.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing CD11b+Ly6G+ liver myeloid subset oscillations at different ZTs (Figure 1A) and 3D microscopy images (Figure 1B).

claim: Neutrophils regulate hepatocyte clock-genes by neutrophil elastase (NE) secretion.
source: Here, we demonstrated that in steady state, neutrophils infiltrated the mouse liver following a circadian pattern and regulated hepatocyte clock-genes by neutrophil elastase (NE) secretion.
evidence: Supported by in vitro experiments showing elastase treatment increases Bmal1 and Clock expression (Figure 1F), and NE-/- mice showing altered clock gene expression (Figure 4B).

claim: NE signals through c-Jun NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) inhibiting fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and activating Bmal1 expression in the hepatocyte.
source: NE signals through c-Jun NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) inhibiting fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and activating Bmal1 expression in the hepatocyte.
evidence: Supported by data showing elastase treatment increases JNK activation (Figure 3C), JNK depletion reduces Bmal1 and increases FGF21 (Figure 3E), and neutropenic mice show lower JNK activation and higher FGF21 (Figure 3A, F).

claim: Mice with neutropenia are protected against steatosis.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by data showing neutropenic mice (MCL1Mrp8-KO) have lower liver triglycerides (Figure 1H) and reduced steatosis after MCD diet (Figure 2H).

claim: Mice with defective neutrophil infiltration are protected against steatosis.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by data showing p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice with impaired neutrophil migration have reduced steatosis (Figure 2H, I) and CXCR2Mrp8-KO mice show protection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).

claim: Mice lacking elastase are protected against steatosis.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by data showing NE-/- mice have lower liver triglycerides after MCD diet (Figure 4D) and HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Protection against steatosis in neutropenic mice correlates with lower JNK activation.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing reduced JNK phosphorylation in neutropenic mice (Figure 3A) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Protection against steatosis in neutropenic mice correlates with reduced Bmal1 expression.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing reduced Bmal1 mRNA in neutropenic mice (Figure 1G) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 2I).

claim: Protection against steatosis in neutropenic mice correlates with increased FGF21 expression.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing increased FGF21 protein in neutropenic mice (Figure 3F) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 3F).

claim: Protection against steatosis in neutropenic mice correlates with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
source: Interestingly, mice with neutropenia, defective neutrophil infiltration or lacking elastase were protected against steatosis correlating with lower JNK activation, reduced Bmal1 and increased FGF21 expression, together with decreased lipogenesis in the liver.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced ACC expression in neutropenic mice (Figure 3A) and reduced Acaca mRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: There is a direct correlation between JNK activation and NE levels in human liver.
source: Lastly, using a cohort of human samples we found a direct correlation between JNK activation, NE levels and Bmal1 expression in the liver.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing JUN and ELANE mRNA levels correlate (r = 0.7362; p = 0.001105) in human livers (Figure 5E).

claim: There is a direct correlation between JNK activation and Bmal1 expression in human liver.
source: Lastly, using a cohort of human samples we found a direct correlation between JNK activation, NE levels and Bmal1 expression in the liver.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing JUN and BMAL1 mRNA levels correlate in human livers (Figure 5E).

claim: There is a direct correlation between NE levels and Bmal1 expression in human liver.
source: Lastly, using a cohort of human samples we found a direct correlation between JNK activation, NE levels and Bmal1 expression in the liver.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing ELANE and BMAL1 mRNA levels correlate (r = 0.6141; p = 0.0052) in human livers (Figure 5E).

claim: Neutrophils contribute to the maintenance of daily hepatic homeostasis through the regulation of the NE/JNK/Bmal1 axis.
source: This study demonstrates that neutrophils contribute to the maintenance of daily hepatic homeostasis through the regulation of the NE/JNK/Bmal1 axis.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including neutrophil depletion studies, elastase knockout studies, JNK inhibition studies, and mechanistic data linking NE to JNK to Bmal1.

claim: Liver neutrophil infiltration peaks at ZT2.
source: Liver neutrophil infiltration showed a clear diurnal pattern, with a peak at ZT2, coinciding with liver-driven lipogenesis in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), and a nadir during the night, at ZT14 (Figure 1A), correlating with lipolysis (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing highest CD11b+Ly6G+ population at ZT2 (Figure 1A).

claim: Liver neutrophil infiltration reaches a nadir at ZT14.
source: Liver neutrophil infiltration showed a clear diurnal pattern, with a peak at ZT2, coinciding with liver-driven lipogenesis in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), and a nadir during the night, at ZT14 (Figure 1A), correlating with lipolysis (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing lowest CD11b+Ly6G+ population at ZT14 (Figure 1A).

claim: The peak of liver neutrophil infiltration at ZT2 coincides with liver-driven lipogenesis in mice.
source: Liver neutrophil infiltration showed a clear diurnal pattern, with a peak at ZT2, coinciding with liver-driven lipogenesis in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), and a nadir during the night, at ZT14 (Figure 1A), correlating with lipolysis (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2015 and data showing higher liver triglycerides at ZT2 (Figure 1D).

claim: The nadir of liver neutrophil infiltration at ZT14 correlates with lipolysis.
source: Liver neutrophil infiltration showed a clear diurnal pattern, with a peak at ZT2, coinciding with liver-driven lipogenesis in mice (Zhou et al., 2015), and a nadir during the night, at ZT14 (Figure 1A), correlating with lipolysis (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2015 and data showing lower liver triglycerides at ZT14 (Figure 1D).

claim: Oscillations in liver neutrophil infiltration correspond directly to changes in neutrophil numbers in blood.
source: These oscillations corresponded directly to changes in neutrophil numbers in blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that liver infiltration might result from higher neutrophil migration to the liver.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing circulating neutrophils oscillate with similar pattern to liver neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Liver infiltration of neutrophils might result from higher neutrophil migration to the liver.
source: These oscillations corresponded directly to changes in neutrophil numbers in blood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that liver infiltration might result from higher neutrophil migration to the liver.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between blood and liver neutrophil oscillations.

claim: Infiltrated neutrophils present an intrasinusoidal distribution in the liver.
source: According to published data (Casanova-Acebes et al., 2018), infiltrated neutrophils presented an intrasinusoidal distribution in the liver, different to that observed in the Kupffer cells population (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D microscopy images showing neutrophil distribution (Figure 1B) and citation to Casanova-Acebes et al., 2018.

claim: The distribution of infiltrated neutrophils in the liver is different from that observed in the Kupffer cells population.
source: According to published data (Casanova-Acebes et al., 2018), infiltrated neutrophils presented an intrasinusoidal distribution in the liver, different to that observed in the Kupffer cells population (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by 3D microscopy images comparing neutrophil (Figure 1B) and Kupffer cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) distributions.

claim: The expression of the hepatocyte-derived neutrophil chemoattractant Cxcl1 is higher at ZT2 than at ZT14.
source: Analysis of liver lysates indicated that the expression of the hepatocyte-derived neutrophil chemoattractant Cxcl1 (Su et al., 2018) was higher at ZT2 than a ZT14.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Cxcl1 mRNA levels at ZT2 and ZT14 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and citation to Su et al., 2018.

claim: Cxcl1 mRNA in liver samples shows the same oscillation pattern as infiltrated neutrophils.
source: Moreover, mRNA of Cxcl1 in liver samples showed the same oscillation pattern than infiltrated neutrophils, suggesting that this chemokine may be important in the regulation of the neutrophil diurnal cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Cxcl1 mRNA oscillations at 6 hr intervals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Cxcl1 may be important in the regulation of the neutrophil diurnal cycle.
source: Moreover, mRNA of Cxcl1 in liver samples showed the same oscillation pattern than infiltrated neutrophils, suggesting that this chemokine may be important in the regulation of the neutrophil diurnal cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between Cxcl1 expression and neutrophil infiltration patterns.

claim: The neutrophil infiltration pattern correlates with liver expression levels of the clock-gene Bmal1.
source: The infiltration pattern correlated with liver expression levels of the clock-gene Bmal1, peaking at ZT2 and bottoming at ZT14 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Bmal1 mRNA levels at different ZTs (Figure 1C).

claim: Liver Bmal1 expression peaks at ZT2.
source: The infiltration pattern correlated with liver expression levels of the clock-gene Bmal1, peaking at ZT2 and bottoming at ZT14 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing highest Bmal1 mRNA at ZT2 (Figure 1C).

claim: Liver Bmal1 expression bottoms at ZT14.
source: The infiltration pattern correlated with liver expression levels of the clock-gene Bmal1, peaking at ZT2 and bottoming at ZT14 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing lowest Bmal1 mRNA at ZT14 (Figure 1C).

claim: Neutrophil infiltration correlates inversely with the expression of Nr1d2, Per2, and Cry2.
source: Infiltration also correlated inversely with the expression of Nr1d2 (encoding Rev-erb β), Per2, and Cry2 (Figure 1C), which are important proteins in the control of circadian rhythms (Reppert and Weaver, 2002), consistent with the feedback loop that controls their expression.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Nr1d2, Per2, and Cry2 mRNA levels at different ZTs (Figure 1C) and citation to Reppert and Weaver, 2002.

claim: Nr1d2, Per2, and Cry2 are important proteins in the control of circadian rhythms.
source: Infiltration also correlated inversely with the expression of Nr1d2 (encoding Rev-erb β), Per2, and Cry2 (Figure 1C), which are important proteins in the control of circadian rhythms (Reppert and Weaver, 2002), consistent with the feedback loop that controls their expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reppert and Weaver, 2002.

claim: Bmal1 is thought to induce lipogenesis.
source: Bmal1 is thought to induce lipogenesis (Zhang et al., 2014), whereas Nr1d2 controls lipid metabolism and its reduced expression promotes lipogenesis and steatosis (Delezie et al., 2012; Solt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Nr1d2 controls lipid metabolism.
source: Bmal1 is thought to induce lipogenesis (Zhang et al., 2014), whereas Nr1d2 controls lipid metabolism and its reduced expression promotes lipogenesis and steatosis (Delezie et al., 2012; Solt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delezie et al., 2012 and Solt et al., 2012.

claim: Reduced expression of Nr1d2 promotes lipogenesis and steatosis.
source: Bmal1 is thought to induce lipogenesis (Zhang et al., 2014), whereas Nr1d2 controls lipid metabolism and its reduced expression promotes lipogenesis and steatosis (Delezie et al., 2012; Solt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delezie et al., 2012 and Solt et al., 2012.

claim: Liver triglycerides are higher at ZT2 than at ZT14.
source: In agreement with these studies, liver triglycerides were higher at ZT2 than at ZT14 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurement data (Figure 1D).

claim: Exposure of mouse hepatocytes in vitro to freshly isolated neutrophils increases hepatocyte expression of Bmal1.
source: Exposure of mouse hepatocytes in vitro to freshly isolated neutrophils increased hepatocyte expression of the clock genes Bmal1 and Clock.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to neutrophils (Figure 1E).

claim: Exposure of mouse hepatocytes in vitro to freshly isolated neutrophils increases hepatocyte expression of Clock.
source: Exposure of mouse hepatocytes in vitro to freshly isolated neutrophils increased hepatocyte expression of the clock genes Bmal1 and Clock.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to neutrophils (Figure 1E).

claim: Exposure of hepatocytes to T or B lymphocytes, or macrophages has no effect on clock gene expression.
source: In contrast, no effect was observed upon exposure to T or B lymphocytes, or macrophages, suggesting the existence of a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication that controls hepatocyte clock-gene expression (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to different immune cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: There exists a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication that controls hepatocyte clock-gene expression.
source: In contrast, no effect was observed upon exposure to T or B lymphocytes, or macrophages, suggesting the existence of a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication that controls hepatocyte clock-gene expression (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on inference from the specific effect of neutrophils but not other immune cells on hepatocyte clock genes.

claim: Neutrophil elastase regulates liver metabolism.
source: We then investigated whether neutrophil elastase (NE), a proteolytic enzyme reported to regulate liver metabolism, could regulate hepatocyte clock genes (Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013 and Talukdar et al., 2012.

claim: Exposure to elastase increases hepatocyte Bmal1 expression.
source: Exposure to elastase reproduced the same increase in hepatocyte Bmal1 and Clock expression in contrast with another protease that did not affect Bmal1 expression (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures treated with elastase (Figure 1F).

claim: Exposure to elastase increases hepatocyte Clock expression.
source: Exposure to elastase reproduced the same increase in hepatocyte Bmal1 and Clock expression in contrast with another protease that did not affect Bmal1 expression (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures treated with elastase (Figure 1F).

claim: Another protease (collagenase) does not affect Bmal1 expression in hepatocytes.
source: Exposure to elastase reproduced the same increase in hepatocyte Bmal1 and Clock expression in contrast with another protease that did not affect Bmal1 expression (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures treated with collagenase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlates with reduced expression of Bmal1 at ZT2.
source: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlated with reduced expression of Bmal1 and Clock (Figure 1G) and increased expression of Cry2 and Per2 at ZT2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice (Figure 1G).

claim: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlates with reduced expression of Clock at ZT2.
source: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlated with reduced expression of Bmal1 and Clock (Figure 1G) and increased expression of Cry2 and Per2 at ZT2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice (Figure 1G).

claim: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlates with increased expression of Cry2 at ZT2.
source: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlated with reduced expression of Bmal1 and Clock (Figure 1G) and increased expression of Cry2 and Per2 at ZT2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice (Figure 1G).

claim: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlates with increased expression of Per2 at ZT2.
source: Low hepatic neutrophil infiltration in neutropenic mice correlated with reduced expression of Bmal1 and Clock (Figure 1G) and increased expression of Cry2 and Per2 at ZT2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice (Figure 1G).

claim: Changes in clock-gene expression in neutropenic mice are accompanied by lower liver triglyceride levels.
source: These changes in clock-gene expression were accompanied by lower liver triglyceride levels (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurement data from neutropenic mice (Figure 1H).

claim: Lack of neutrophils perturbs the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1 expression in the liver.
source: Furthermore, lack of neutrophils perturbed the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1, Clock, and Per2 expression in the liver without affecting clock genes in other organs such as the lung, in which there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing altered Bmal1 oscillations in neutropenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Lack of neutrophils perturbs the diurnal rhythmicity in Clock expression in the liver.
source: Furthermore, lack of neutrophils perturbed the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1, Clock, and Per2 expression in the liver without affecting clock genes in other organs such as the lung, in which there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing altered Clock oscillations in neutropenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Lack of neutrophils perturbs the diurnal rhythmicity in Per2 expression in the liver.
source: Furthermore, lack of neutrophils perturbed the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1, Clock, and Per2 expression in the liver without affecting clock genes in other organs such as the lung, in which there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing altered Per2 oscillations in neutropenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: Lack of neutrophils does not affect clock genes in the lung.
source: Furthermore, lack of neutrophils perturbed the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1, Clock, and Per2 expression in the liver without affecting clock genes in other organs such as the lung, in which there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no change in lung Bmal1 in neutropenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).

claim: In the lung, there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression.
source: Furthermore, lack of neutrophils perturbed the diurnal rhythmicity in Bmal1, Clock, and Per2 expression in the liver without affecting clock genes in other organs such as the lung, in which there is no correlation between the peak of neutrophil infiltration and Bmal1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and qRT-PCR data from lung samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Neutrophils might specifically control the expression of hepatocyte circadian clock genes in steady state.
source: Our results thus indicate that neutrophils might specifically control the expression of hepatocyte circadian clock genes in steady state.
evidence: Based on inference from the liver-specific effects of neutrophil depletion on clock genes.

claim: Chronic jet lag alters liver circadian genes.
source: Chronic jet lag alters liver circadian genes and disrupts liver metabolism (Kettner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kettner et al., 2016.

claim: Chronic jet lag disrupts liver metabolism.
source: Chronic jet lag alters liver circadian genes and disrupts liver metabolism (Kettner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kettner et al., 2016.

claim: Jet lag causes complete disruption of the circadian liver neutrophil infiltration.
source: Analysis of a mouse model of jet lag revealed complete disruption of the circadian liver neutrophil infiltration with increased hepatic neutrophil infiltration even at ZT14 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing loss of neutrophil oscillations in jet-lagged mice (Figure 2A).

claim: Jet lag increases hepatic neutrophil infiltration at ZT14.
source: Analysis of a mouse model of jet lag revealed complete disruption of the circadian liver neutrophil infiltration with increased hepatic neutrophil infiltration even at ZT14 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing elevated neutrophils at ZT14 in jet-lagged mice (Figure 2A).

claim: Abolition of rhythmic neutrophil hepatic infiltration under jet lag correlates with increased steatosis.
source: Abolition of rhythmic neutrophil hepatic infiltration under jet lag correlated with increased steatosis and high levels of liver triglycerides (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from jet-lagged mice (Figure 2B).

claim: Abolition of rhythmic neutrophil hepatic infiltration under jet lag correlates with high levels of liver triglycerides.
source: Abolition of rhythmic neutrophil hepatic infiltration under jet lag correlated with increased steatosis and high levels of liver triglycerides (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements from jet-lagged mice (Figure 2B).

claim: Jet lag-induced steatosis is less severe in neutropenic mice.
source: Jet lag-induced steatosis was less severe in neutropenic mice (Figure 2C), and disruption of diurnal liver expression of Bmal1 detected in control jet-lagged mice was partially ablated in neutropenic mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from neutropenic jet-lagged mice (Figure 2C).

claim: Disruption of diurnal liver expression of Bmal1 in jet-lagged mice is partially ablated in neutropenic mice.
source: Jet lag-induced steatosis was less severe in neutropenic mice (Figure 2C), and disruption of diurnal liver expression of Bmal1 detected in control jet-lagged mice was partially ablated in neutropenic mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing Bmal1 expression in neutropenic jet-lagged mice (Figure 2D).

claim: Mice with impaired neutrophil migration (Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice) show reduced neutrophil infiltration that correlates with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression.
source: Similar results were also observed in mice with impaired neutrophil migration such as Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Eash et al., 2010; Mei et al., 2012) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (González-Terán et al., 2016). In both models, the reduction of neutrophil infiltration correlated with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression and protection from jet lag-induced steatosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and citations to Eash et al., 2010 and Mei et al., 2012.

claim: Mice with impaired neutrophil migration (p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice) show reduced neutrophil infiltration that correlates with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression.
source: Similar results were also observed in mice with impaired neutrophil migration such as Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Eash et al., 2010; Mei et al., 2012) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (González-Terán et al., 2016). In both models, the reduction of neutrophil infiltration correlated with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression and protection from jet lag-induced steatosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) and citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: Reduction of neutrophil infiltration in Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice correlates with protection from jet lag-induced steatosis.
source: Similar results were also observed in mice with impaired neutrophil migration such as Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Eash et al., 2010; Mei et al., 2012) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (González-Terán et al., 2016). In both models, the reduction of neutrophil infiltration correlated with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression and protection from jet lag-induced steatosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Reduction of neutrophil infiltration in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice correlates with protection from jet lag-induced steatosis.
source: Similar results were also observed in mice with impaired neutrophil migration such as Cxcr2MRP8-KO BM transplanted mice (Eash et al., 2010; Mei et al., 2012) and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (González-Terán et al., 2016). In both models, the reduction of neutrophil infiltration correlated with decreased levels of liver Bmal1 expression and protection from jet lag-induced steatosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Inflammation plays a key role in the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: Inflammation plays a key role in the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Tiniakos et al., 2010) and the development of hepatic steatosis is associated with increased liver infiltration by myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils (González-Terán et al., 2016; Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012; Tiniakos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tiniakos et al., 2010.

claim: The development of hepatic steatosis is associated with increased liver infiltration by myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils.
source: Inflammation plays a key role in the pathogenesis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (Tiniakos et al., 2010) and the development of hepatic steatosis is associated with increased liver infiltration by myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils (González-Terán et al., 2016; Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012; Tiniakos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to González-Terán et al., 2016; Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012; Tiniakos et al., 2010.

claim: High-fat diet (HFD) increases liver neutrophil infiltration in WT mice at ZT2, ZT14, and ZT18.
source: Two widely used mouse models of hepatic steatosis, high-fat diet (HFD) and methionine-choline-deficient (MCD) diet, increased liver neutrophil infiltration in WT mice at ZT2, ZT14, and ZT18 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophils in HFD-fed mice (Figure 2E).

claim: Methionine-choline-deficient (MCD) diet increases liver neutrophil infiltration in WT mice at ZT2, ZT14, and ZT18.
source: Two widely used mouse models of hepatic steatosis, high-fat diet (HFD) and methionine-choline-deficient (MCD) diet, increased liver neutrophil infiltration in WT mice at ZT2, ZT14, and ZT18 (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophils in MCD-fed mice (Figure 2E) and immunofluorescence images (Figure 2F).

claim: MCD diet enhances Bmal1 expression in control mice at ZT2.
source: Consistent with a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication in the regulation of hepatocyte clock genes, the MCD diet enhanced Bmal1 expression and inhibited Cry2 and Per2 expression in control mice, but not in neutropenic mice at ZT2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from MCD-fed control mice (Figure 2G).

claim: MCD diet inhibits Cry2 expression in control mice at ZT2.
source: Consistent with a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication in the regulation of hepatocyte clock genes, the MCD diet enhanced Bmal1 expression and inhibited Cry2 and Per2 expression in control mice, but not in neutropenic mice at ZT2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from MCD-fed control mice (Figure 2G).

claim: MCD diet inhibits Per2 expression in control mice at ZT2.
source: Consistent with a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication in the regulation of hepatocyte clock genes, the MCD diet enhanced Bmal1 expression and inhibited Cry2 and Per2 expression in control mice, but not in neutropenic mice at ZT2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from MCD-fed control mice (Figure 2G).

claim: MCD diet does not alter clock gene expression in neutropenic mice at ZT2.
source: Consistent with a neutrophil-to-hepatocyte communication in the regulation of hepatocyte clock genes, the MCD diet enhanced Bmal1 expression and inhibited Cry2 and Per2 expression in control mice, but not in neutropenic mice at ZT2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from MCD-fed neutropenic mice (Figure 2G).

claim: Altered liver clock-gene regulation in neutropenic mice is associated with protection against steatosis.
source: Altered liver clock-gene regulation in neutropenic mice was associated with protection against steatosis and lower liver triglycerides (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from neutropenic mice fed MCD diet (Figure 2H).

claim: Altered liver clock-gene regulation in neutropenic mice is associated with lower liver triglycerides.
source: Altered liver clock-gene regulation in neutropenic mice was associated with protection against steatosis and lower liver triglycerides (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements from neutropenic mice fed MCD diet (Figure 2H).

claim: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduces circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from anti-Ly6G treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: Anti-Ly6G treatment for 21 days markedly decreases hepatic diurnal Bmal1 expression.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from anti-Ly6G treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Anti-Ly6G treatment for 21 days markedly decreases hepatic diurnal Clock expression.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from anti-Ly6G treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Anti-Ly6G treatment for 21 days increases expression of Cry2.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from anti-Ly6G treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Anti-Ly6G treatment for 21 days increases expression of Per2.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from anti-Ly6G treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Anti-Ly6G treatment for 21 days reduces steatosis.
source: Anti-Ly6G administration for 7 days reduced circulating neutrophil levels without affecting monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and treatment for 21 days markedly decreased hepatic diurnal Bmal1 and Clock expression, increased expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) and consequently reduced steatosis (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice exhibit deficient neutrophil migration.
source: To further support the role of neutrophil liver infiltration in the regulation of liver clock genes and hepatic lipogenesis during diet-induced steatosis, we leveraged a mouse model (p38γ/δLyzs-KO) that exhibits deficient neutrophil migration and subsequently, reduced liver neutrophil infiltration after MCD diet (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice have reduced liver neutrophil infiltration after MCD diet.
source: To further support the role of neutrophil liver infiltration in the regulation of liver clock genes and hepatic lipogenesis during diet-induced steatosis, we leveraged a mouse model (p38γ/δLyzs-KO) that exhibits deficient neutrophil migration and subsequently, reduced liver neutrophil infiltration after MCD diet (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice show hepatic down-regulation of Bmal1 compared with diet-matched control mice.
source: Compared with diet-matched control (Lyzs-Cre) mice, MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice showed hepatic down-regulation of Bmal1, which was associated with higher expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice fed MCD diet (Figure 2I).

claim: Down-regulation of Bmal1 in MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice is associated with higher expression of Cry2.
source: Compared with diet-matched control (Lyzs-Cre) mice, MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice showed hepatic down-regulation of Bmal1, which was associated with higher expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice fed MCD diet (Figure 2I).

claim: Down-regulation of Bmal1 in MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice is associated with higher expression of Per2.
source: Compared with diet-matched control (Lyzs-Cre) mice, MCD-diet-fed p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice showed hepatic down-regulation of Bmal1, which was associated with higher expression of Cry2, and Per2 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice fed MCD diet (Figure 2I).

claim: The reduced neutrophil infiltration in mice lacking myeloid p38γ/δ expression is responsible for the altered expression of circadian clock genes.
source: These results suggest that the reduced neutrophil infiltration in mice lacking myeloid p38γ/δ expression is responsible for the altered expression of circadian clock genes.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlation between reduced neutrophil infiltration and altered clock gene expression in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration modulates clock-gene expression in the liver, with downstream effects on liver metabolism.
source: Overall, these findings strongly support that neutrophil infiltration modulates clock-gene expression in the liver, with downstream effects on liver metabolism.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental models showing neutrophil effects on clock genes and metabolism.

claim: JNK activation in the liver may be regulated in a circadian manner with a peak at noon.
source: It has been suggested that JNK activation in the liver may be regulated in a circadian manner with a peak at noon (Robles et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robles et al., 2014.

claim: Lack of neutrophils is associated with lower liver expression of JNK.
source: Lack of neutrophils was associated with lower liver expression and activation of JNK, lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun, and lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acaca), a key enzyme in metabolic regulation (acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ACC) that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from neutropenic mice (Figure 3A).

claim: Lack of neutrophils is associated with lower activation of JNK.
source: Lack of neutrophils was associated with lower liver expression and activation of JNK, lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun, and lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acaca), a key enzyme in metabolic regulation (acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ACC) that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing reduced phospho-JNK in neutropenic mice (Figure 3A).

claim: Lack of neutrophils is associated with lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun.
source: Lack of neutrophils was associated with lower liver expression and activation of JNK, lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun, and lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acaca), a key enzyme in metabolic regulation (acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ACC) that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing reduced phospho-c-Jun in neutropenic mice (Figure 3A).

claim: Lack of neutrophils is associated with lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC).
source: Lack of neutrophils was associated with lower liver expression and activation of JNK, lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun, and lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acaca), a key enzyme in metabolic regulation (acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ACC) that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing reduced Acaca mRNA in neutropenic mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: ACC is a key enzyme in metabolic regulation that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis.
source: Lack of neutrophils was associated with lower liver expression and activation of JNK, lower activation of the JNK downstream effector c-Jun, and lower expression of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (Acaca), a key enzyme in metabolic regulation (acetyl-CoA carboxylase; ACC) that mediates inhibition of beta-oxidation and activation of lipid biosynthesis (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ACC function.

claim: Reduced liver neutrophil infiltration in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice is associated with decreased JNK phosphorylation.
source: Similar results were found in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice, in which reduced liver neutrophil infiltration was associated with decreased JNK phosphorylation and ACC protein levels (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Reduced liver neutrophil infiltration in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice is associated with decreased ACC protein levels.
source: Similar results were found in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice, in which reduced liver neutrophil infiltration was associated with decreased JNK phosphorylation and ACC protein levels (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Neutrophil-treated hepatocytes show increased JNK activation.
source: Moreover, neutrophil-treated hepatocytes showed increased JNK activation together with increased levels of ACC expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Neutrophil-treated hepatocytes show increased levels of ACC expression.
source: Moreover, neutrophil-treated hepatocytes showed increased JNK activation together with increased levels of ACC expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Elastase-treated hepatocytes show higher JNK activation.
source: NE represents a potential mediator of this neutrophil function because elastase-treated hepatocytes also showed higher JNK activation, suggesting that this protease modulates the expression of the clock genes through the JNK signaling pathways (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from hepatocyte cultures treated with elastase (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Elastase modulates the expression of clock genes through the JNK signaling pathways.
source: NE represents a potential mediator of this neutrophil function because elastase-treated hepatocytes also showed higher JNK activation, suggesting that this protease modulates the expression of the clock genes through the JNK signaling pathways (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that elastase increases JNK activation and Bmal1 expression.

claim: JNK activation by elastase is accompanied by increased Bmal1 expression.
source: This JNK activation was accompanied by increased Bmal1 expression (Figure 3D), indicating that neutrophils altered liver clock-gene expression through the elastase-JNK pathway.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from elastase-treated hepatocytes (Figure 3D).

claim: Neutrophils alter liver clock-gene expression through the elastase-JNK pathway.
source: This JNK activation was accompanied by increased Bmal1 expression (Figure 3D), indicating that neutrophils altered liver clock-gene expression through the elastase-JNK pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined effects of elastase on JNK and Bmal1.

claim: JNK is an important modulator of the expression of the hepatokine circadian regulator FGF21.
source: JNK is an important modulator of the expression of the hepatokine circadian regulator FGF21 (Vernia et al., 2014), which controls glucose and lipid metabolism (Fisher and Maratos-Flier, 2013; Li et al., 2013; Potthoff et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vernia et al., 2014.

claim: FGF21 controls glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: JNK is an important modulator of the expression of the hepatokine circadian regulator FGF21 (Vernia et al., 2014), which controls glucose and lipid metabolism (Fisher and Maratos-Flier, 2013; Li et al., 2013; Potthoff et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fisher and Maratos-Flier, 2013; Li et al., 2013; Potthoff et al., 2012.

claim: Mice lacking JNK in hepatocytes have higher FGF21 mRNA expression.
source: Mice lacking JNK in hepatocytes had higher FGF21 mRNA expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from JNK1/2Alb-KO mice (Figure 3E).

claim: FGF21 expression is reduced in neutrophil-exposed hepatocytes.
source: In concordance with high JNK activation, FGF21 expression was reduced in neutrophil-exposed hepatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from hepatocyte cultures exposed to neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Neutropenic mice show increased FGF21 expression.
source: Moreover, neutropenic and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice showed increased FGF21 expression (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J), which was consistent with the reduced hepatocyte JNK activation in these mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from neutropenic mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).

claim: p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice show increased FGF21 expression.
source: Moreover, neutropenic and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice showed increased FGF21 expression (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J), which was consistent with the reduced hepatocyte JNK activation in these mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).

claim: The protection of p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice against MCD-diet-induced alterations is abrogated by shFGF21.
source: The protection of p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice against MCD-diet-induced alterations was abrogated by shFGF21 and these mice developed steatosis with an elevated hepatic triglyceride content (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice infected with shFGF21 (Figure 3H, I).

claim: p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice infected with shFGF21 develop steatosis with elevated hepatic triglyceride content.
source: The protection of p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice against MCD-diet-induced alterations was abrogated by shFGF21 and these mice developed steatosis with an elevated hepatic triglyceride content (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice infected with shFGF21 (Figure 3H, I).

claim: Neutrophil infiltration controls liver metabolism through the regulation of FGF21 expression.
source: These data further supported the idea that neutrophil infiltration controls liver metabolism through the regulation of FGF21 expression.
evidence: Based on inference from the FGF21 knockdown experiments reversing the protective effects of reduced neutrophil infiltration.

claim: NE levels in liver are higher at ZT2 than at ZT14 in WT mice fed a normal diet.
source: To formally confirm the involvement of NE in circadian clock alteration, we first evaluated the diurnal oscillation of NE levels in liver from WT mice fed a normal diet (ND). According to infiltration pattern of neutrophils in the liver (Figure 1A), we found higher NE levels at ZT2 than at ZT14. (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of extracellular NE in liver (Figure 4A).

claim: NE-/- mice have lower Bmal1 expression compared to control mice.
source: Next, circadian clock-gene expression in NE-/- mice revealed lower Bmal1 and elevated Per2 and Cry2 expression, compared to control mice (Figure 4B), which mimicked the behavior of neutropenic mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice (Figure 4B).

claim: NE-/- mice have elevated Per2 expression compared to control mice.
source: Next, circadian clock-gene expression in NE-/- mice revealed lower Bmal1 and elevated Per2 and Cry2 expression, compared to control mice (Figure 4B), which mimicked the behavior of neutropenic mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice (Figure 4B).

claim: NE-/- mice have elevated Cry2 expression compared to control mice.
source: Next, circadian clock-gene expression in NE-/- mice revealed lower Bmal1 and elevated Per2 and Cry2 expression, compared to control mice (Figure 4B), which mimicked the behavior of neutropenic mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice (Figure 4B).

claim: Clock gene expression in NE-/- mice mimics the behavior of neutropenic mice.
source: Next, circadian clock-gene expression in NE-/- mice revealed lower Bmal1 and elevated Per2 and Cry2 expression, compared to control mice (Figure 4B), which mimicked the behavior of neutropenic mice.
evidence: Based on inference from the similarity in clock gene expression patterns between NE-/- and neutropenic mice.

claim: NE-/- mice present lower respiratory quotient during the lights-on period than WT mice.
source: In addition, NE-/- mice presented lower respiratory quotient during the lights-on period than WT mice, indicating that these mice have increased fat utilization as a source of energy (Figure 4C), supporting the data that reduced liver-neutrophil infiltration results in higher lipid oxidation.
evidence: Supported by respiratory exchange ratio measurements (Figure 4C).

claim: NE-/- mice have increased fat utilization as a source of energy.
source: In addition, NE-/- mice presented lower respiratory quotient during the lights-on period than WT mice, indicating that these mice have increased fat utilization as a source of energy (Figure 4C), supporting the data that reduced liver-neutrophil infiltration results in higher lipid oxidation.
evidence: Based on inference from the lower respiratory quotient in NE-/- mice.

claim: Reduced liver-neutrophil infiltration results in higher lipid oxidation.
source: In addition, NE-/- mice presented lower respiratory quotient during the lights-on period than WT mice, indicating that these mice have increased fat utilization as a source of energy (Figure 4C), supporting the data that reduced liver-neutrophil infiltration results in higher lipid oxidation.
evidence: Based on inference from the metabolic phenotype of NE-/- mice.

claim: NE-/- mice are protected against steatosis when fed MCD diet.
source: Interestingly, when fed MCD or HFD diet, NE-/- mice were protected against steatosis (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), presented lower JNK activation, and expressed less ACC than control mice (Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4D, E).

claim: NE-/- mice are protected against steatosis when fed HFD.
source: Interestingly, when fed MCD or HFD diet, NE-/- mice were protected against steatosis (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), presented lower JNK activation, and expressed less ACC than control mice (Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from NE-/- mice fed HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: NE-/- mice present lower JNK activation than control mice when fed MCD or HFD diet.
source: Interestingly, when fed MCD or HFD diet, NE-/- mice were protected against steatosis (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), presented lower JNK activation, and expressed less ACC than control mice (Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4F) and HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: NE-/- mice express less ACC than control mice when fed MCD or HFD diet.
source: Interestingly, when fed MCD or HFD diet, NE-/- mice were protected against steatosis (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), presented lower JNK activation, and expressed less ACC than control mice (Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4G) and HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: NE-/- mice are protected against alterations in clock-gene expression induced by MCD diet.
source: Besides, NE-/- mice were protected against alterations in clock-gene expression induced by MCD diet, presenting lower expression of Bmal1 and higher of Cry2 and Per2 comparing to control mice at ZT2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4H).

claim: NE-/- mice fed MCD diet present lower expression of Bmal1 compared to control mice at ZT2.
source: Besides, NE-/- mice were protected against alterations in clock-gene expression induced by MCD diet, presenting lower expression of Bmal1 and higher of Cry2 and Per2 comparing to control mice at ZT2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4H).

claim: NE-/- mice fed MCD diet present higher expression of Cry2 compared to control mice at ZT2.
source: Besides, NE-/- mice were protected against alterations in clock-gene expression induced by MCD diet, presenting lower expression of Bmal1 and higher of Cry2 and Per2 comparing to control mice at ZT2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4H).

claim: NE-/- mice fed MCD diet present higher expression of Per2 compared to control mice at ZT2.
source: Besides, NE-/- mice were protected against alterations in clock-gene expression induced by MCD diet, presenting lower expression of Bmal1 and higher of Cry2 and Per2 comparing to control mice at ZT2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice fed MCD diet (Figure 4H).

claim: Under HFD, NE-/- mice maintain a pattern of clock-gene expression similar to control mice on normal diet.
source: Furthermore, under HFD, NE-/- mice were also refractory to these changes as these mice maintained a pattern of clock-gene expression similar to control mice in ND (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from NE-/- mice fed HFD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Infusion of WT neutrophils increases Bmal1 expression in the liver of neutropenic mice after jet lag.
source: The infusion of WT neutrophils was able to increase Bmal1 expression in the liver after jet lag, while neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils presented the same levels of Bmal1 than non-infused neutropenic mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice infused with WT neutrophils (Figure 5B).

claim: Neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils present the same levels of Bmal1 as non-infused neutropenic mice after jet lag.
source: The infusion of WT neutrophils was able to increase Bmal1 expression in the liver after jet lag, while neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils presented the same levels of Bmal1 than non-infused neutropenic mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils (Figure 5B).

claim: Infusion of neutropenic mice with WT neutrophils increases steatosis.
source: In addition, while infusion of neutropenic mice with WT neutrophils increased steatosis, neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils presented the same levels of steatosis than control neutropenic mice (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from neutropenic mice infused with WT neutrophils (Figure 5C, D).

claim: Neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils present the same levels of steatosis as control neutropenic mice.
source: In addition, while infusion of neutropenic mice with WT neutrophils increased steatosis, neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils presented the same levels of steatosis than control neutropenic mice (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements and histology from neutropenic mice infused with NE-/- neutrophils (Figure 5C, D).

claim: Diet or jet-lag-induced hepatic infiltration of neutrophils results in dysregulation of the liver clock.
source: All these data indicate that diet or jet-lag -induced hepatic infiltration of neutrophils results in dysregulation of the liver clock, and the lack of NE is enough to protect mice against these alterations.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental models showing neutrophil effects on clock genes under different conditions.

claim: The lack of NE is enough to protect mice against diet or jet-lag-induced alterations in liver clock.
source: All these data indicate that diet or jet-lag -induced hepatic infiltration of neutrophils results in dysregulation of the liver clock, and the lack of NE is enough to protect mice against these alterations.
evidence: Based on inference from the protective effects observed in NE-/- mice and neutrophil infusion experiments.

claim: The levels of ELANE expression directly correlate with BMAL1 mRNA in human livers.
source: Our results suggest that the levels of ELANE expression directly correlate with BMAL1 and JUN mRNA in livers from a human cohort (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing r = 0.6141; p = 0.0052 between ELANE and BMAL1 (Figure 5E).

claim: The levels of ELANE expression directly correlate with JUN mRNA in human livers.
source: Our results suggest that the levels of ELANE expression directly correlate with BMAL1 and JUN mRNA in livers from a human cohort (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing r = 0.7362; p = 0.001105 between ELANE and JUN (Figure 5E).

claim: Rhythmic neutrophil infiltration in the liver controls the expression of clock genes through the JNK pathway activation.
source: These correlations reinforce the idea that a rhythmic neutrophil infiltration in the liver controls the expression of clock genes through the JNK pathway activation and could be a target for therapeutic intervention during non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: Based on inference from the correlations observed in human samples and the mechanistic data from mouse models.

claim: Rhythmic neutrophil infiltration in the liver could be a target for therapeutic intervention during non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: These correlations reinforce the idea that a rhythmic neutrophil infiltration in the liver controls the expression of clock genes through the JNK pathway activation and could be a target for therapeutic intervention during non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: Based on speculation about therapeutic implications of the findings.

claim: Neutrophils control clock genes in the liver.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that neutrophils control clock genes in the liver and that reduced neutrophil infiltration protects against jet lag and diet-induced liver steatosis by altering the expression of these temporal regulators.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including neutrophil depletion, elastase knockout, and in vitro studies.

claim: Reduced neutrophil infiltration protects against jet lag-induced liver steatosis by altering the expression of clock genes.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that neutrophils control clock genes in the liver and that reduced neutrophil infiltration protects against jet lag and diet-induced liver steatosis by altering the expression of these temporal regulators.
evidence: Supported by data from neutropenic and p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice under jet lag conditions.

claim: Reduced neutrophil infiltration protects against diet-induced liver steatosis by altering the expression of clock genes.
source: Our analysis demonstrates that neutrophils control clock genes in the liver and that reduced neutrophil infiltration protects against jet lag and diet-induced liver steatosis by altering the expression of these temporal regulators.
evidence: Supported by data from neutropenic, p38γ/δLyzs-KO, and NE-/- mice fed MCD or HFD.

claim: At least part of neutrophil-induced clock modulation is mediated by elastase.
source: Our results also demonstrate that at least part of this neutrophil-induced clock modulation is mediated by elastase.
evidence: Supported by data from NE-/- mice and elastase treatment experiments.

claim: NE mediates the deleterious effects of neutrophils on liver metabolism.
source: These results agree with previous data showing that NE mediates the deleterious effects of neutrophils on liver metabolism and that mice lacking NE are protected against diet-induced steatosis (Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013 and Talukdar et al., 2012.

claim: Mice lacking NE are protected against diet-induced steatosis.
source: These results agree with previous data showing that NE mediates the deleterious effects of neutrophils on liver metabolism and that mice lacking NE are protected against diet-induced steatosis (Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013; Talukdar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mansuy-Aubert et al., 2013 and Talukdar et al., 2012, and data from current study (Figure 4D, E).

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying neutrophil regulation of liver metabolism involves neutrophil NE that induces activation of JNK.
source: The molecular mechanism underlying this regulation involves neutrophil NE that induces activation of JNK and consequently inhibits the production of the hepatokine FGF21.
evidence: Supported by data showing elastase increases JNK activation (Figure 3C) and NE-/- mice have lower JNK activation (Figure 4F).

claim: Neutrophil NE activation of JNK consequently inhibits the production of the hepatokine FGF21.
source: The molecular mechanism underlying this regulation involves neutrophil NE that induces activation of JNK and consequently inhibits the production of the hepatokine FGF21.
evidence: Supported by data showing JNK deletion increases FGF21 (Figure 3E) and neutropenic mice have higher FGF21 (Figure 3F).

claim: The JNK pathway is an important modulator of liver metabolism.
source: The JNK pathway is an important modulator of liver metabolism, and lack of JNK1 and JNK2 in hepatocytes protects against steatosis (Manieri and Sabio, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manieri and Sabio, 2015.

claim: Lack of JNK1 and JNK2 in hepatocytes protects against steatosis.
source: The JNK pathway is an important modulator of liver metabolism, and lack of JNK1 and JNK2 in hepatocytes protects against steatosis (Manieri and Sabio, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manieri and Sabio, 2015.

claim: JNK regulates hepatocyte clock genes.
source: Here, we also demonstrate that JNK also regulates hepatocyte clock genes and, therefore, modulates diurnal adaptation of liver metabolism.
evidence: Supported by data showing JNK deletion reduces Bmal1 and Clock expression (Figure 3E).

claim: JNK modulates diurnal adaptation of liver metabolism.
source: Here, we also demonstrate that JNK also regulates hepatocyte clock genes and, therefore, modulates diurnal adaptation of liver metabolism.
evidence: Based on inference from JNK's regulation of clock genes and metabolic enzymes.

claim: Lipogenesis is increased in the light phase.
source: Recently published data have demonstrated that lipogenesis is increased in the light phase, in agreement with our analysis (Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guan et al., 2018 and data showing higher triglycerides at ZT2 (Figure 1D).

claim: Neutrophil infiltration causes JNK activation downstream of elastase secretion, a time-dependent process.
source: We show that neutrophil infiltration causes JNK activation down-stream of elastase secretion, a time-dependent process.
evidence: Supported by data showing elastase increases JNK activation (Figure 3C) and neutrophil infiltration correlates with JNK activation.

claim: Phosphoproteomic analysis of the hepatic phosphorylation network identifies JNK as a key signaling enzyme with peak activation at ZT6.
source: Indeed, phosphoproteomic analysis of the hepatic phosphorylation network identifies JNK as a key signaling enzyme with peak activation at ZT6 (Robles et al., 2017) immediately prior to the peak of lipogenic gene expression (Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robles et al., 2017.

claim: The peak of lipogenic gene expression occurs after ZT6.
source: Indeed, phosphoproteomic analysis of the hepatic phosphorylation network identifies JNK as a key signaling enzyme with peak activation at ZT6 (Robles et al., 2017) immediately prior to the peak of lipogenic gene expression (Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guan et al., 2018.

claim: Neutrophils induce an accumulative activation of JNK with a peak during the day that would control the lipogenic program.
source: Our results suggest that neutrophils induce an accumulative activation of JNK with a peak during the day that would control the lipogenic program.
evidence: Based on inference from the timing of neutrophil infiltration, JNK activation, and lipogenic gene expression.

claim: The metabolic effects of JNK in the liver are mediated by FGF21.
source: Recent evidence established that the metabolic effects of JNK in the liver are mediated by FGF21 (Vernia et al., 2016; Vernia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vernia et al., 2016 and Vernia et al., 2014.

claim: Liver FGF21 expression can be modulated through the control of JNK by neutrophils.
source: Our results now show that liver FGF21 expression can be modulated through the control of JNK by neutrophils.
evidence: Supported by data showing neutropenic mice have higher FGF21 (Figure 3F) and neutrophil-treated hepatocytes have lower FGF21 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).

claim: Reduction of FGF21 by shRNA reverts the protective effect of reduced neutrophil infiltration.
source: Reduction of FGF21 by shRNA reverted the protective effect and metabolic changes induced by reduced neutrophil infiltration.
evidence: Supported by data showing FGF21 knockdown in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice restores steatosis (Figure 3H, I).

claim: Reduction of FGF21 by shRNA reverts the metabolic changes induced by reduced neutrophil infiltration.
source: Reduction of FGF21 by shRNA reverted the protective effect and metabolic changes induced by reduced neutrophil infiltration.
evidence: Supported by data showing FGF21 knockdown in p38γ/δLyzs-KO mice restores steatosis (Figure 3H, I).

claim: The diurnal oscillating migratory properties of neutrophils regulate liver function in a manner that preserves daily metabolic rhythms.
source: In conclusion, our results show that the diurnal oscillating migratory properties of neutrophils regulate liver function in a manner that preserves daily metabolic rhythms, and that disturbance of this rhythmicity can cause disease.
evidence: Based on inference from the collective findings showing neutrophil effects on clock genes and metabolism.

claim: Disturbance of neutrophil rhythmicity can cause disease.
